query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a modest Nb addition (≈5 at%) into a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will lead to the formation of fine, uniformly distributed Nb-rich precipitates (e.g., Ni3Nb-like intermetallics) that improve high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance compared to the same alloy without Nb.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the principal constituents (with remaining elements adjusted to satisfy the HEA definition of 5–35 at% each) and that exhibits a single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Add approximately 5 at% niobium (Nb) to the baseline alloy composition while keeping the overall equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios required for HEAs.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature service conditions (e.g., 700°C to 1100°C) in an inert or controlled atmosphere, using conventional thermal processing to achieve homogeneity.
generation.structural_mediator: The controlled precipitation of fine Nb-rich intermetallic phases (such as a Ni3Nb-type phase) within a titanium-nickel matrix.
generation.mechanism: Nb acts as a secondary phase former: its addition encourages the in situ formation of a nanoscale precipitate phase that effectively hinders dislocation movement (precipitation hardening) and improves microstructural stability at high temperatures, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Elevated-temperature mechanical tests will show higher yield strength and improved creep resistance in the Nb-added alloy relative to the baseline titanium-nickel primary HEA.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without the ~5 at% Nb addition, exhibiting a single-phase solid solution.
generation.boundary: The alloy must remain within the HEA composition limits (each element between 5–35 at%) with Nb limited to around 5 at%; performance is predicted under high-temperature conditions typical of aerospace or similar extreme applications.
generation.uncertainty: The specific morphology, size, and distribution of the precipitates, as well as potential trade-offs in ductility or oxidation resistance, depend on processing and heat-treatment parameters and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one set of the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary HEA and a second set with an added 5 at% Nb. Process both sets identically through casting and heat treatment. Conduct microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM, XRD) to determine precipitate formation and phase distribution. Perform mechanical tests (elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests) at target temperatures (e.g., 900°C).
measurements: Creep resistance metrics (e.g., creep rate under constant load)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-added alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the formation of fine, uniformly distributed Nb-rich precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: With the development of high-temperature metallic materials, Ni-based superalloys have been unable to meet the requirements of aerospace engines. It is urgent to find a new high-performance alloy to replace the Ni-based superalloy []. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) based on refractory elements with superior high-temperature mechanical properties have recently attracted intensive research attention, which are regarded as promising candidates for high-temperature structural materials [,,]. However, their inferior plasticity along with high ductile–brittle transition temperature and high density seriously limits their aerospace applications, where the requirements are mainly focus on the deformability and high specific strength of alloys.

Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites [].
